content.title: About
content.content: Raw cactus (typically Opuntia species, commonly called "nopal" or "prickly pear pads") are edible young stems of the cactus plant, popular in Mexican and South American cuisines. They have a crisp texture and a mildly tangy‑sweet flavor, and are eaten fresh, in salads, pickles, or lightly sautéed.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cactus pads are up to 90 % water, making them very refreshing in hot climates.
In Mexican cuisine they are called "nopal", while in Spanish they are often referred to as "prickly pear" pads.
The edible pads are covered with tiny spines that are usually removed before consumption.
Native peoples of North America have used cactus as food, medicine, and building material for centuries.
More than 150 Opuntia species are edible, with Opuntia ficus‑indica being the most widely cultivated.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Cactus pads provide both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: One cup of sliced raw cactus contains about 30 kcal, making it an excellent choice for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Raw cactus is a source of vitamins C, A, K and minerals such as magnesium, calcium, and potassium.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytonutrients like betacyanins give cactus its bright color and act as antioxidants.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C and polysaccharides in cactus help strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cactus, ranging from itching to swelling or hives.

items.title: Sharp spines
items.content: Improperly cleaned pads may retain tiny spines that can injure the mouth or throat.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large amounts of raw cactus can cause gas and bloating due to its high fiber content.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: If grown conventionally, cactus should be thoroughly rinsed to remove possible pesticide residues.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Typically the pads are de‑spined, sliced, and eaten raw in salads, pickles, or with a squeeze of lime. They can also be lightly sautéed, added to omelets, tacos, or soups. Soaking the pads in cold water for 15‑20 minutes before preparation helps reduce any residual bitterness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh cactus pads in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze them in portion‑sized bags; they retain their texture after thawing.
